systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

The Impact of Climate Change on Fisheries
Fabio Cevenini, Christopher Costello, and Carlo Fezzi
NBER Working Paper No. 35994
November 2026
JEL No. Q22, Q54
ABSTRACT
This paper provides the first causal estimate of the effect of ocean temperature variations on fishing 
revenue. We develop a simple theoretical model underpinning an empirical specification estimated 
on 2.5 million spatially explicit observations of fishing revenue from all European vessels for 
2013–2022. The identification strategy leverages a novel metric, Marine Degree Days, which 
quantifies species-specific temperature exposure relative to biologically established thermal 
tolerance intervals. Within this framework we address key identification challenges, including 
spatial selection and ecological interdependencies across species. We find that deviations from 
species’ thermal preferences lead to significant losses in fishing revenue, with heat exposure 
causing the most pronounced impacts. These effects are mediated by species’ vertical mobility and 
ecological characteristics. Projections across different climate scenarios point to widespread 
revenue declines by 2100, reaching €560 million annual losses in the warmest scenario, though 
impacts are highly spatially heterogeneous. Lower-income, equatorial areas are expected to suffer 
the most, while some colder regions experience gains.

1 Introduction
There is mounting evidence on the effects of weather and climate on economic outcomes, such as agricultural output
(Burke & Emerick, 2016; Moscona & Sastry, 2023; Schlenker et al., 2006; Waldinger, 2022), labour productivity
(Graff Zivin & Neidell, 2014; Somanathan et al., 2021) and economic growth (Acevedo et al., 2020; Bilal & K¨ anzig,
2026; Dell et al., 2012). Temperature changes have been found to have a tangible impact also on mortality (Carleton
et al., 2022; Deschˆ enes & Greenstone, 2011), violence (Card & Dahl, 2011; Harari & Ferrara, 2018) and mental
health (Burke et al., 2018). These studies have shaped both scientific and policy debates by translating current
and future climatic variation into economic impacts (see Auffhammer, 2018; Carleton and Hsiang, 2016; Dell et al.,
2014 for reviews). Yet, this empirical literature has largely overlooked the ocean, despite its central role in both
the climatic and economic systems. As a result, we still know relatively little about the economic consequences of
global warming on marine fisheries, one of the world’s most important natural production systems.
Marine fisheries generate hundreds of billions of dollars in revenue globally (F AO, 2025), supporting more than
62 million jobs worldwide across harvesting, processing, trade, and coastal services (F AO, 2024). They also sustain
the livelihood of about 10% of the global population by playing a central role in food security, particularly in
developing countries (Costello et al., 2020). Arguably, the scarcity of causal evidence on the impact of climate
change on fisheries reflects two obstacles that characterize the marine environment. The first one is severe data
limitations (Costello et al., 2012). Compared to terrestrial sectors like agriculture, fisheries outcomes have been
recorded less consistently, are less standardized across countries, and often lack fine geographic detail, especially
over long time spans. Second, the intrinsic complexities of the marine system pose unique challenges for causal
identification. Fish stocks are not directly observed, can move across space, and interact dynamically with both
their environment and other species. Finally, fishers’ adaptation strategies respond not only to realized weather,
but also to expected returns and to information about forthcoming conditions, such as weather forecasts, which can
shape effort, timing, and location choices (Shrader, 2023; M. D. Smith, 2005). From an econometric perspective,
these features introduce complex forms of sample selection, spillovers, and potential omitted variable bias that make
standard empirical strategies difficult to implement.
This paper addresses this research gap by providing the first causal estimate of the effect of ocean temperature on
marine fisheries revenue. We address the challenges above by leveraging a novel, high-resolution dataset including
more than 2.5 million observations of annual, spatially-located fishing revenue, spanning the Atlantic Ocean, the
Arctic, and the Mediterranean Sea. These spatial data contain information about the fishing activities carried out
between 2013 and 2022 by the universe of vessels registered in countries belonging to the European Union, including
records of all the species caught and the characteristics of the fishing fleet such as vessel length, fishing technique
and fishing gear used. These metrics are stored at a 0.5 x 0.5 spatial grid resolution ( ∼ 55 x 55 km at the equator)
annually.
We merge these data with two other sources of information. First, recognizing that fish physiology depends on
1
temperature, we match each cell-year with its local thermal conditions represented by daily, remotely sensed, sea
surface temperature (SST). Second, recognizing that warming may affect each species differently, we collect species-
level biological information, most notably their thermal preference ranges (Cheung et al., 2013). These data enable
us to map a single spatial temperature realization to the heterogeneous levels of exposure experienced by all the
species residing in that location. Specifically, we translate SST into species-specific exposure by developing a novel
metric inspired by the degree-day measure used in agricultural and energy economics (see Hogan and Schlenker,
2024 for an overview), which we call Marine Degree Day (MDD). This new indicator cumulates the exposure to
temperatures outside the preferred thermal interval of each species. The key insight provided by this metric is that
the same sea temperature can be beneficial for one species and harmful for another, depending on their different
thermal tolerances. For each species, we consider the degree days above their thermal range (denoted by M DD+)
and the degree days below their thermal range (denoted by M DD−). These measures reflect both the intensity
and the duration of ocean temperature dynamics, while embedding biological and ecological heterogeneity in two
easily interpretable indexes.
Our empirical design directly estimates the impact of MDDs on the fishing revenue for each species, exploiting
the exogenous variation in exposure. Intuitively, the identification of the causal effect of temperature on fishing
revenue comes from two underlying comparisons. First, our strategy compares outcomes for different species caught
by the same vessel and technology types in the same location and year. Second, we compare revenue for the same
species but in neighboring locations that contain the same management environment. In all analyses, we include a
high-dimensional fixed-effects specification that absorbs (i) all determinants of revenue that vary at the cell-by-year
level, such as fishers’ selection and effort in different fishing locations, technology and local determinants such as
the ecological habitat or the presence of a marine protected area, and (ii) all shocks that are common to the same
species-by-year-by-management region, such as management constraints at the relevant regulatory scale and market
conditions such as input and output prices.
Our empirical specification is underpinned by a stylized bio-economic model that links ocean temperature to
fishing revenue through fish population dynamics. In this model, temperature shifts local habitat conditions and
changes the system’s carrying capacity, i.e. the amount of fish biomass the environment can sustain given its
ecological limits. A change in carrying capacity alters biological growth and the evolution of biomass over time,
which affects the sustainable harvest rate and, therefore, revenue. Our model maps temperature to biological growth
via carrying capacity, while the sustainable management objectives from EU fishing regulations allow us to link
changes in carrying capacity to changes in target biomass. This structural framework resolves our primary empirical
problem: the inability to directly observe fish stocks.
We find that thermal exposure outside species’ preferred ranges generates significant and asymmetric damages.
Both heat and cold exposure generate reductions in fishing revenue, but the estimated effect of exposure above
the range is approximately three times that of exposure below it. When we allow for non-linear effects, we find
that the marginal effect of heat exposure becomes significantly more harmful at higher temperatures, confirming
2
that extremely warm conditions can generate disproportionate biological and economic impacts (Fr¨ olicher et al.,
2018; K. E. Smith et al., 2023), while the damage from cold is approximately linear over the observed range of
our data. We also document different sources of heterogeneity underpinned by plausible biological mechanisms of
adaptation including vertical mobility in the water column and ecological group. These results remain coherent
under a broad set of robustness checks, including potential spillovers across space, ecological spillovers across
species, specifications that allow species-specific responses to habitat characteristics and spatial gradients, and
many alternative specifications, variable definitions and samples.
Finally, we combine the estimated dose-response function with daily temperature projections under two different
climate scenarios to quantify the implied consequences of ocean warming on fisheries revenue through 2100. Our
projections imply widespread declines under higher-emissions pathways, with substantial spatial heterogeneity.
Under the most pessimistic scenario, we project losses of approximately €560 million per year by the end of the
century. Such losses are concentrated in already warm areas, while colder regions experience smaller damages or
even gains. This spatial pattern implies that damages are disproportionately concentrated in areas with lower-
income, highlighting a marine dimension of climate inequality that is largely absent from the existing literature
(Cain et al., 2024).
Our findings extend the climate economics literature by providing the first direct causal estimate of the effect of
ocean temperature on fisheries revenue. While a large scientific literature has documented the biological impacts of
ocean warming on marine ecosystems (Cheung et al., 2013; Hoegh-Guldberg & Bruno, 2010; Sumaila et al., 2011),
only a few studies have attempted to quantify its economic consequences (Barange et al., 2014; Cheung et al., 2010,
2021, 2026; Gaines et al., 2018; Lam et al., 2016). These contributions differ in their modeling details but share
a common approach. They start from a biological model that translates ocean warming into predicted changes
in biomass and potential catches, and then convert biological outcomes into economic ones by applying a back-of-
the-envelope calculation assuming prices, fishing effort and management regimes as fixed. This simulation-based
approach is useful for identifying vulnerable species and regions, but it does not rely on realized outcomes and
therefore cannot capture fishers’ adaptation or other complexities that are only revealed through careful empirical
analysis. In particular, it abstracts from the ways in which changes in behavior, technology, and regulation mediate
ecological pressures into realized catches and revenue. In contrast, our approach estimates how revenue responds to
temperatures using realized data, so the effects we recover already embed the influence of market conditions, effort
adjustments and management rules.
Our paper also contributes to a growing literature examining how keystone animal species influence economic
outcomes (Alsan, 2015; Feir et al., 2024; Frank & Sudarshan, 2024). All these studies focus on the presence,
disappearance, or local collapse of a single species of particular relevance, documenting effects on outcomes such
as disease spread, agricultural production, occupational structure, and long-run economic development. In this
paper we extend this literature by taking into account biological diversity across multiple species within the same
ecosystem, while also considering their relevant ecological interactions. In our setting, diversity in fishes’ thermal
3
preferences becomes a primary mediator of the impact of climate change on fisheries. To our knowledge, this is the
first paper to incorporate this type of ecological complexity into empirical economic analysis.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the data sources and the construction
of the MDD metrics. Section 3 introduces the theoretical framework that links SST to fishing revenue. Section 4
presents the empirical strategy. Section 5, 6, and 7 present the main results and the robustness checks. Section 8
provides projections under alternative climate scenarios. Section 9 concludes with policy implications and directions
for future research.
2 Data
We construct a unique dataset by integrating information from several sources: fisheries revenue data from the
Scientific, Technical, and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF) of the European Union, satellite SST data
from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and data on fish species and ocean
characteristics from different biological sources. We also get SST daily climate projections from the Earth System
Model Version 4.1 (ESM4), developed by the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL) of NOAA. We
provide a concise description of each data source below.
2.1 Fisheries revenue data
We use the spatial fishing dataset provided by the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries
(STECF) of the European Union. The dataset reports catches and ex-vessel revenue for all EU fishing vessels
operating under the EU Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) over the period 2013-2022.
The EU CFP is the main framework governing fisheries management in EU waters and, operationally, aims to
keep exploitation rates consistent with their Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY), i.e., the largest long-run harvest
that can be sustained without depleting the stock. The CFP measures are defined for each biological stock within a
delineated management area: in other words, management is spatially explicit, and the relevant regulatory unit is
a stock (species) inside a management area. Supplemental Appendix A.1 illustrates the type of management-area
delineations observed in our data for an illustrative region (North Sea and Baltic Sea). These management areas
align with Food and Agriculture Organization (F AO) fishing divisions and related statistical subdivisions.
In compliance with the reporting obligations under the CFP and the EU Data Collection Framework, each
vessel must record the location of fishing activity, landed quantities by species, and the fishing technology and gear
used. These trip-level records are compiled and harmonized in the STECF spatial product. Revenue is calculated
using ex-vessel prices , i.e., the prices received by fishers at first sale when the catch enters the supply chain. A
key feature of the STECF spatial data is that revenue is spatially geo-localized on the C-SQUARES grid (Concise
Spatial QUery And REpresentation System), a global geocode system designed to enable simple spatial indexing
of marine information (Rees, 2003). Grid cells have size 0 .5◦ × 0.5◦ (about 55 km at the equator), providing a very
4
fine resolution for the fisheries context.
Within each cell, observations are further disaggregated by species, vessel length class (e.g., 18-24 m), fishing
technique (e.g., purse seine, bottom trawling) and fishing gear (e.g. trammel nets, boat dredges). Supplemental
Appendix A.2, A.3 and A.4 provide the complete lists of vessel length classes, fishing techniques and gear types
included in the dataset. On the biological dimension, the dataset covers a very broad range of species, including
small pelagics (e.g., sardine, anchovy, mackerel), large pelagics (e.g., tunas), demersal finfish (e.g., cod, hake) and
benthic organisms (e.g., cephalopods and crustaceans). While the raw data include more than 3,000 species and
aquatic organisms, commercial value is concentrated in a relatively small subset. Consequently, we focus on the top
100 species (by value) which together account for about 95% of total revenue (Supplemental Appendix A.5 lists the
included species). While these data are released with quarterly frequency, we aggregate them at the yearly level to
abstract from within-year seasonality and align the analysis with the frequency of most management instruments.
Figure 1 presents the geographic distribution of the revenue data. The dataset includes fishing activity in both
EU waters and non-EU Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs).1 This reflects the fact that EU fleets can operate beyond
EU jurisdiction under bilateral agreements, such as reciprocal access. The dataset also includes fishing activity in
international waters. EU overseas territories also generate limited observations in other ocean basins (e.g., Indian
Ocean and Pacific Ocean) but, given their sparse nature (less than 4% of total revenue), we exclude them from the
main analysis. Therefore, our baseline geographic domain includes all observations within F AO Major Fishing Areas
27 (North-East Atlantic), 21 (North-West Atlantic), 31 (Western Central Atlantic), 34 (Eastern Central Atlantic),
37 (Mediterranean and Black Sea), 41 (South-West Atlantic), and 47 (South-East Atlantic). 2
1An EEZ is a sea region, extending up to 200 nautical miles (approximately 370 km) from a coastal state’s baselines, within which
the coastal state holds sovereign rights over the exploration and exploitation of marine resources, including fisheries.
2We perform several additional cleaning steps to address residual inconsistencies in the data. These procedures, documented in

2.2 Sea surface temperature and thermal preferences
We measure ocean temperature using daily SST from the NOAA Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature
(OISST) Analysis v2.1 (Huang et al., 2021). OISST provides global daily SST gridded data at the 0 .25◦ × 0.25◦
spatial resolution ( ∼ 25km × 25km), calculated from satellite observations corrected with in situ measurements
(ships, buoys, and Argo floats).
These data are available globally and constructed consistently over time. Our analysis employs daily temperature
data for the 2013-2022 period, matching the time span of our fishing information.
To link temperature to fishing activity, we harmonize OISST data to the spatial resolution of our fishing dataset
(c-square cells), calculating for each cell i and day d the relevant weighted average SST. Figure 2 presents the
resulting variability in average SST across the F AO macro-areas in our sample, showing how mean temperature
ranges differ substantially across areas. Our data effectively mirror the global spectrum of SST, encompassing
temperatures from sub-zero conditions up to nearly 30 ◦C. As expected, temperature is strongly related to latitude,
and semi-enclosed basins (e.g. the Mediterranean) display a less variable distribution relative to open-ocean regions.
Figure 2: Distribution of the average SST (2013-2022) across the macro-regions (F AO areas) in our data.
We combine daily SST with species-level information on thermal preferences, defined as the SST range in which
a species is typically found. Our main source of information is Cheung et al. (2013), which reports the interquartile
range of SST preferences for more than 900 species of fish, shellfish, and crustaceans. For the five species in
our sample not covered by Cheung et al. (2013), we use thermal ranges from FishBase (www.fishbase.org) and
SeaLifeBase (www.sealifebase.org), two comprehensive and regularly updated repositories of biological information
on marine species. These estimates rely on the AquaMaps framework, which combines occurrence records with
ecological constraints from the literature to infer species-specific environmental envelopes, including temperature
7
tolerance bounds. Table A.6 in Supplemental Appendix A.5 reports the thermal range for each species included in
the data.
It is worth noting that, although fish inhabit various depths of the water column and, therefore, experience
temperatures that differ from our SST, this does not pose a problem for our analysis for two key reasons. First,
thermal preferences are already expressed in terms of SST, thereby inherently accounting for depth-related temper-
ature gradients. Second, the cell-specific day-to-day variability of SST is highly correlated with the corresponding

Projecting differences from the 2013-2022 baseline holds fixed all the non-temperature determinants of revenue
absorbed by our fixed effects (e.g., price conditions, fuel costs, regulations and enforcement, fleet composition, and
other common shocks), so that our scenarios should be interpreted ceteris paribus and not as predictions of the
future. To avoid extrapolating the estimated temperature-response function beyond the support of the data, we
constrain projected thermal exposure to the range observed in the estimation sample, replacing values outside this
range with the nearest observed boundary (Auffhammer et al., 2013; Fezzi & Bateman, 2015). This adjustment
affects less than 0.1% of projected observations.
Considering the potential channels of fishers’ adaptation, a key feature of our setting is that fishing activity
conducted within the spatial boundaries of our analysis is regulated under the Common Fisheries Policy (and
related bilateral agreements), whose operational objective is to keep exploitation rates consistent with MSY (EU,
2013). For our projections, this implies that adaptation operates within an institutional constraint. For each species,
the management adjusts the aggregate harvest quota in response to stock conditions and scientific advice, while
fishers can adapt only within the constraint implied by that quota. When quotas are fully utilized, additional fishing
effort cannot offset temperature-induced reductions in the total allowable catch, as aggregate harvest is constrained
by regulation. However, when quotas are not fully utilized, fishers may have greater scope to compensate for
declining productivity by increasing effort or adjusting their fishing strategies. Unused quotas do not necessarily
imply effective adaptation opportunities, as catches may remain constrained by stock availability, fishing costs, or
other operational limitations. Nevertheless, where feasible, adjustments in fishing effort could provide a margin of
adaptation, potentially mitigating some of the projected revenue losses associated with climate change.
Another potential margin of adaptation involves gradual shifts, such as expansion into new fishing grounds. In
our projections, we exclude such spatial shifts and maintain the geographic boundaries defined by our data. This
approach is akin to the assumption implemented in the agricultural economics literature, which holds total land
area constant when calculating climate change projections (Burke & Emerick, 2016). Furthermore, a large-scale
reallocation of effort across fishing grounds is unlikely since policy trends point toward greater spatial restrictions
rather than expansion. Proposals to restrict fishing in the high seas are gaining traction (Roberts et al., 2025), and
29
marine protected areas are expanding globally (McDonald et al., 2024). Taken together, these forces suggest that
wild fisheries are more likely to be compressed than to find substantial new space.
A final concern is that climate change may induce long-run shifts in species distributions. Our cell-level projec-
tions hold the species present in a cell fixed to those observed during the baseline years. In other words, in each given
cell, species already present can decline significantly, potentially approaching zero, but species that are currently
absent cannot enter the cell. The projections may therefore understate local species replacement as suitable habi-
tats shift. Available evidence suggests such species displacements to be limited, with changes in species-distribution
centroids or boundaries averaging approximately 5–7 km per year (Garc ´ ıa Molinos et al., 2016), making this feature
unlikely to affect our results. However, we explore its relevance by recalculating our climate change projection at
the management-area level, using the estimates in Table 3. Management areas combine, on average, more than
50 individual 0 .5◦ × 0.5◦ cells and have a median area of approximately 160,000 km2. This aggregation allows
projections to draw on a much broader set of species historically observed within each area and, therefore, allows
much more significant species redistribution. The results, which are reported in Supplemental Appendix E, leave
the main conclusions unchanged.
8.2 Projected impacts
Figure 7 presents predicted percentage changes for each of the two scenarios, grouped into three time windows
(2026-2050, 2051-2075, and 2076-2100). Each boxplot represents the distribution of 25 values of yearly aggregated
revenue changes and, therefore, illustrates year-to-year variability within each scenario and time frame and not
model uncertainty. Median effects are negative in both scenarios and become more severe over time. In the first
time period (2026-2050), median losses are modest, around 2% in both scenarios. By mid-century (2051-2075),
damages increase to roughly 5% under SSP-2.45 and 6% under SSP-3.70. By the last quarter of the century (2076-
2100), the divergence between the two scenarios becomes clearer: median losses are around 8% under SSP-2.45 and
about 12% under SSP-3.70.
Figure 8 reports the same results as a continuous time series, expressed in billions of euros relative to the
2013-2022 baseline (baseline aggregate revenue in our study area is approximately 4.5 billion euros per year). Our
projections show that the two scenarios remain relatively close in the first half of the century and diverge after
mid-century. In the near term, ocean warming is limited and the reduction in cold exposure can partially offset
the increase in heat exposure, yielding relatively small aggregate changes. As warming strengthens, heat exposure
grows rapidly and dominates our impacts, since our estimated effects are markedly asymmetric. By the end of
the century, losses reach around 430 million euros per year under SSP-2.45 and around 560 million euros per year
under SSP-3.70. The shaded confidence intervals are obtained from 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations drawing the
model coefficients from their estimated joint distribution. These intervals widen toward the end of the century as
projected temperatures diverge from the current ones.
Figure 9 maps projected impacts at the cell level, highlighting the strong spatial heterogeneity across scenarios
30
and horizons (2051-2075 in the top panel; 2076-2100 in the bottom panel). In the open Atlantic, impacts display
a clear north-south gradient. By mid-century (2051-2075), tropical and subtropical waters exhibit large projected

visible under SSP-3.70, especially in the late-century period (2076-2100), where parts of the Arctic, sub-Arctic and
mid-Atlantic experience increases on the order of 10% to 20%, consistent with reductions in cold exposure more
than offsetting the increase in heat exposure. In contrast, coastal and semi-enclosed seas near Europe experience
predominantly reductions in revenue across both scenarios, with damages intensifying in later decades. An impor-
tant implication of this spatial pattern is distributional: the largest losses are concentrated in lower-latitude regions,
especially along the West African Atlantic, where projected damages are particularly severe under SSP-3.70. Since
these ocean regions tend to be the most accessible to developing countries along the West African coast, our results
highlight the unequal burden of climate-change impacts. The figure reports cell-level point estimates, while in
Table E.1 of Supplemental Appendix E we report the 95% confidence intervals for spatially aggregated impacts at
the F AO-area level.
Finally, Figure 10 reports late-century (2076-2100) projections for the 15 species generating the highest baseline
revenue. Most species experience substantial declines, but there is meaningful heterogeneity. For example, Norway
lobster is projected to benefit slightly under SSP-3.70, reflecting the fact that its catches are concentrated in colder
waters where reduced cold exposure can generate a positive impact. At the other extreme, blue and red shrimp and
European pilchard are among the most heavily affected species, with median losses exceeding 25% under SSP-3.70.
Other sizable late-century losses include Atlantic herring, European plaice, European sprat, Atlantic cod, common
shrimp, and Atlantic horse mackerel. Under SSP-2.45, the ranking of affected species is broadly similar, although
losses are less severe. Importantly, even relatively small percentage declines can translate into substantial absolute
losses for high-value species such as Atlantic mackerel, which accounts for the largest share of baseline revenue.

9 Discussion and conclusion
This paper estimates the causal impact of ocean temperature on fisheries revenue. Exposure to temperatures outside
a species’ preferred thermal range affects its carrying capacity, ultimately reducing its stock biomass. Therefore,
deviations from species’ preferred temperature ranges, both colder and warmer, reduce revenue, but the impact
of heat exposure is almost three times stronger than the impact of cold exposure. Prior evidence shows that low
temperatures can slow feeding and growth, especially for warm-adapted species (Reid et al., 2022). On the other
hand, heat exposure creates a broader set of risks including habitat disruption (for example through coral bleaching)
and lower oxygen availability in the water column (Alfonso et al., 2021).
Our results show that heat exposure becomes especially damaging when temperatures exceed the upper bound
of the thermal range by a large margin (i.e. more than 5 ◦C). This pattern is consistent with evidence that extreme
warming events, e.g. marine heatwaves, can trigger large and persistent disruptions in marine ecosystems (K. E.
Smith et al., 2023). This is particularly relevant given that marine heatwaves are projected to become more frequent
and intense under climate change (Fr¨ olicher et al., 2018).
We also show that a species’ ability to move vertically within the water column mitigates the impact of thermal
exposure, especially for heat anomalies. This is consistent with the idea that species can exploit the vertical
temperature gradients to buffer the thermal stress. For this reason, incorporating the vertical thermal gradient in
the characterization of exposure and responses may become increasingly important as deoxygenation alters habitat
quality at depth (Fredston et al., 2023).
We also estimate meaningful heterogeneity across ecological groups. Demersal species, which live near the seabed,
appear particularly vulnerable to both warming and cooling. Pelagic species, which occupy the open water column,
are more resilient, plausibly because they can adjust their distribution more easily in response to temperature shifts.
Finally, invertebrates, such as clams, cuttlefish or squid, show the highest resilience of all ecological categories we
examined.
Turning to climate change impact projections, our scenarios provide a clear picture of how, ceteris paribus,
climate change will affect fisheries. While magnitudes vary across scenarios and regions, the overall pattern points
to negative aggregate impacts. We estimate a strong geographic heterogeneity, implying that climate change will
create both winners and losers, as in other sectors such as agriculture (Auffhammer, 2018; Fezzi & Bateman, 2015;
Schlenker et al., 2006). High-latitude and cold Atlantic regions may experience revenue gains, raising the importance
of international cooperation and governance to manage shifting and newly accessible resources. By contrast, warmer
ocean regions and enclosed seas such as the Mediterranean and Baltic are projected to face large losses, calling for
region-specific adaptation strategies and support for vulnerable fishing communities.
From a policy perspective, this heterogeneity may suggest prioritizing adaptive management where risks are the
greatest. In settings where warming shifts productivity across space and species, policies that facilitate adjustment,
such as flexible quota allocations and incentives to diversify target portfolios, may reduce costs, though our study was
34
unable to test these adjustments directly. The divergence in outcomes across scenarios after 2050 also underscores
the value of mitigation.
Our projections can be compared to earlier simulation-based studies of climate impacts on global fisheries
(Barange et al., 2014; Cheung et al., 2010, 2021; Lam et al., 2016). These studies confirm our conclusion that
climate change will generate both winners and losers, but our quantitative projections differ in important ways.
Relative to such studies, our projections are less severe by mid century. In particular, compared with Lam et al.
(2016), we estimate modest aggregate losses by 2050, and compared with Cheung et al. (2010) and Barange et al.
(2014) we find weaker spatial heterogeneity at mid century, even though the end of century spatial pattern is
qualitatively similar (losses in enclosed and low latitude seas and gains at higher latitudes). Our interpretation is
that simulation-based approaches may overstate both positive and negative changes relative to what is implied by
realized economic outcomes. This is consistent with the fact that such approaches typically abstract from adaptation
margins.
Finally, our approach comes with its own caveats. First, because we project differences from the 2013-2022
baseline, our results are conditional on institutional and market conditions, including prices and demand conditions,
input costs, and fleet composition. In the long run, these are all possible margins of adaptation. Second, while
realized outcomes embed the short-run behavioral and institutional adjustments observed in the data, they do not
capture slower, structural adaptations that may matter over longer horizons, such as major technological change,
durable shifts in targeting and spatial access, or reforms to the Common Fisheries Policy that alter harvest caps and
allocation rules. A natural extension for future research would be to refine our projections by explicitly modeling
how fishing effort and spatial quota allocation respond to temperature, also beyond the geographical extent of our
dataset.
